title: 0/1 Knapsack
directAnswer: Given items with weights and values and a capacity W, maximize total value where each item is taken at most once. The recurrence is dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]]) — either skip item i or take it. Naive recursion is O(2ⁿ); memoize on (i, w) or build a 2-D table for O(nW). Then collapse to a 1-D dp[w] and iterate weight DESCENDING so each item is used once.

remember.pattern: 0/1 knapsack — take-or-skip on a 2-D (item, capacity) grid
remember.formula:
dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]                              # skip item i
         = max(that, val[i] + dp[i-1][w - wt[i]])  # take item i, if wt[i] <= w
1-D: for each item, for w from W down to wt[i]: dp[w] = max(dp[w], val[i] + dp[w - wt[i]])
rules: Two choices per item: **skip** (carry `dp[i-1][w]`) or **take** (`val[i] + dp[i-1][w - wt[i]]`). Take is only legal when `wt[i] <= w`.
Each item is used **at most once** — that's the '0/1'. The take branch reads row `i-1`, never row `i`, so it can't reuse the same item.
In the 1-D optimization, iterate weight **DESCENDING** (`W → wt[i]`). Ascending would let an item be picked twice, turning it into unbounded knapsack.
Initialize `dp[0][*] = 0` and `dp[*][0] = 0` — zero items or zero capacity yields zero value.
Answer is `dp[n][W]`. The grid is `(n+1) × (W+1)`; the off-by-one from the empty-prefix row 0 trips people up.
whenToUse: Pick a subset to maximize value under a single capacity/budget constraint
Each item is available exactly once (no repeats)
Two-way decision per element: include it or leave it
Constraint and values are small enough that O(nW) is affordable (pseudo-polynomial)
antiSignals: Items reusable unlimited times → unbounded knapsack, iterate weight ASCENDING
You only need feasibility (does a subset hit an exact sum?) → Subset Sum boolean DP
Capacity W is astronomically large → O(nW) is too big; consider meet-in-the-middle or branch-and-bound
Fractions of an item allowed → greedy by value/weight ratio (fractional knapsack), not DP
remember.takeaway: 0/1 Knapsack is the parent of an entire family. Burn the take-or-skip recurrence into memory: dp[i][w] = max(skip, value + dp[i-1][w - weight]). Subset Sum, Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum, and Last Stone Weight II are all this same grid with the objective swapped. The DESCENDING 1-D sweep is the single trick that separates 0/1 from unbounded.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model a constrained optimization as a 2-D DP over (items, capacity), derive the take-or-skip recurrence cleanly, and know why the 1-D space optimization must iterate capacity backwards.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Iterating weight ascending in the 1-D version (silently allows reusing an item, computing the unbounded answer), or reading the current row instead of the previous row in the take branch.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the recurrence from the include/exclude decision, show the 2-D table, then collapse to 1-D and explain — out loud — that descending order is what enforces 'each item once'. Name the parent pattern and its children (Subset Sum, Partition, Target Sum).

problemStatement:
You are given `n` items, where item `i` has a positive weight `weight[i]` and a positive value `value[i]`, and a knapsack with a maximum weight capacity `W`.

Choose a ***subset*** of the items so that the total weight is at most `W` and the ***total value is maximized***. Each item may be used **at most once** (you either take it whole or leave it — no fractions, no repeats).

Return the maximum total value achievable.
constraints: All weights and values are integers
understanding: From a fixed set of items, pick a subset whose weights sum to at most W while the value sum is as large as possible. The decision is binary per item — in or out — which is exactly why it's called 0/1. It is the textbook constrained subset-optimization problem and the root of the whole knapsack family.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I use an item more than once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — at most once each. That's the 0/1 constraint. If items were reusable it would be unbounded knapsack, and the 1-D loop direction would flip.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I take a fraction of an item?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Fractional knapsack is a different (greedy) problem solved by value/weight ratio. Here it's whole-item or nothing.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are weights and values guaranteed positive integers?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Integer weights are what make the capacity axis a finite, indexable dimension — the basis of the O(nW) table.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if no item fits (every weight > W)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The answer is 0 — taking nothing is always a valid subset with value 0. The base row/column handles this automatically.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can W get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 10⁴ here, so an O(nW) table of ~10⁶ cells is fine. If W were ~10⁹ the table approach would be infeasible and we'd need a different technique.

examples.explanation: Take items with weights 3 and 4 (values 4 + 5 = 9). Total weight 7 fits exactly. The weight-5 item alone gives only 7.
Items weight 2 + 3 = 5 give value 3 + 4 = 7. Taking the weight-4 item leaves capacity for nothing else (value 5).
Nothing fits in capacity 3, so the best subset is empty with value 0.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. 0/1 Knapsack lands on the 2-D-then-1-D table branch.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recursive Include/Exclude
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to establish the take-or-skip recurrence, then flag the 2ⁿ branching before optimizing.
hints: Focus on the LAST item. You only ever do one of two things with it: leave it out, or put it in. What subproblem remains in each case?
If you skip item i, you must still fill capacity w from items 0..i-1. If you take it (only when weight[i] ≤ w), you gain value[i] and fill w - weight[i] from items 0..i-1.
knap(i, w) = max(knap(i-1, w), value[i] + knap(i-1, w - weight[i])). Base case: no items left (i < 0) → value 0.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every item forks into take/skip, so the recursion tree has up to 2ⁿ leaves. Each node does O(1) work. Recursion depth is n, giving O(n) stack space.
approaches.explanation:
Decide the items one at a time, from the last index down to the first. For item `i` there are exactly two futures: **exclude** it and solve the same capacity `w` using items `0..i-1`, or **include** it (only legal when `weight[i] <= w`), collect `value[i]`, and solve the reduced capacity `w - weight[i]` using items `0..i-1`. The answer for `(i, w)` is the larger of those two.

**The mental shift: one binary decision, then recurse on a smaller item set.** Don't try to choose the whole subset at once. Commit to a single item's fate, shrink the problem by one item, and let recursion handle the rest. Because the include branch recurses on `i-1` (not `i`), the same item can never be picked twice — that single detail is what encodes the '0/1' rule.

**Why the take branch is guarded by `weight[i] <= w`.** You can't put an item into a knapsack that no longer has room for it. If `weight[i] > w`, the take branch is simply unavailable and only the skip branch survives — there's no negative-capacity subproblem.

**Why max, not sum.** We're choosing the *best* of two mutually exclusive plans (with vs without item `i`), so we combine them with `max`. Summing would double-count plans that are alternatives, not companions.

**Why we don't ship this.** The same `(i, w)` state is reached through enormously many take/skip orderings, so the tree recomputes it over and over — exponential overlap. Cache the answer per `(i, w)` and the blowup collapses.
approaches.insight: The state is fully described by two numbers: how many items remain to decide (i) and how much capacity is left (w). Two small state variables plus massive recomputation is the textbook signal to memoize over a 2-D grid.

dryRun.intro: knap(i, w) = max(skip, take). Decide items from the last index down. Notice knap(0, w) gets reached from multiple branches.

java.explanation: Base case: no items left to decide — an empty subset has value 0.

java.line: int skip = solve(weight, value, i - 1, w);
java.explanation: Leave item i out — capacity unchanged, move to the previous item.
Only allow the take branch when the item actually fits — no negative capacity.

java.line: take = value[i] + solve(weight, value, i - 1, w - weight[i]);
java.explanation: Take item i: gain its value, recurse on i-1 (so it's never reused) with reduced capacity.

python.explanation: No items remain — base case returns 0 value.
Exclude the current item; same capacity, previous item index.
Guard the include branch so we never index a negative remaining capacity.
Pick the better of the two mutually exclusive plans.

edgeCases.behavior: Every take branch is blocked (weight ≥ 1 > 0), so every path returns 0 — empty knapsack.

pitfalls: Recursing on i (not i-1) in the take branch — lets an item be reused, which solves unbounded knapsack instead.
Forgetting the weight[i] <= w guard — produces a negative-capacity subproblem.
Skipping this approach as 'too obvious' — the include/exclude recurrence is exactly what the interviewer wants you to verbalize first.

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization on (item, capacity)
approaches.whenToMention: The fix once you name the overlap — 'cache the answer for each (item, capacity) pair'.
hints: solve(i, w) returns the same value every time it's called with the same arguments. Where can you store it so each pair is computed once?
Use a 2-D memo of size n × (W+1), indexed by item and remaining capacity. Check it on entry; fill it before returning.
memo[i][w] = max(skip, take). Use a sentinel like -1 for 'uncomputed' since 0 is a legitimate answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are n × (W+1) distinct (i, w) states. Each is computed once with O(1) work → O(nW) time. The memo table is O(nW); recursion depth is O(n) on top of that.
approaches.explanation:
Keep the take-or-skip recurrence, but cache `solve(i, w)` in a 2-D table so every `(item, capacity)` pair is solved exactly once. The memo starts 'uncomputed'; on entry we return the cached value, and we store the result before returning.

**The mental shift: the future depends only on (i, w).** Whatever sequence of take/skip choices led here, the remaining decisions depend solely on which items are still undecided (`i`) and how much room is left (`w`). Two different paths that both reach `(2, 5)` have identical futures, so caching by `(i, w)` collapses all those duplicate subtrees into one computation. The number of distinct states — `n × (W+1)` — is exactly the time bound.

**Why a 2-D memo, not 1-D.** Unlike Coin Change (where the only state is the remaining amount), here the answer genuinely depends on *both* the item index and the capacity, because which items are still available changes the answer. Drop the `i` dimension and you'd conflate states with different remaining item sets.

**Why -1 as the sentinel.** A value of 0 is a perfectly valid answer (nothing fits), so 0 cannot mean 'uncomputed'. Initialize the memo to -1 and treat that as the empty marker.

**A language note worth saying out loud.** This top-down form recurses up to `n` deep. In Java that's fine for `n ≤ 100`. In Python the default recursion limit is about 1000, so deep top-down DP can hit `RecursionError` on large inputs — which is exactly why the bottom-up table (next approach) is the safer default in Python.
approaches.insight: Memoization is the same mechanical upgrade as every DP: a correct recurrence plus a cache keyed on the true state. The intellectual work was recognizing that `(item index, remaining capacity)` is the complete state — once you see that, the table writes itself, and its size is your time complexity.

dryRun.intro: memo[i][w] caches the best value using items 0..i within capacity w. Filled lazily from the last item down.

steps.action: best of items 0..2 in cap 7 → wt3+wt4 = 4+5 = 9

java.explanation: -1 marks 'uncomputed'. 0 can't be the sentinel because an empty knapsack legitimately scores 0.
Cache hit — return the stored best value for this (item, capacity) in O(1).

java.line: take = value[i] + solve(weight, value, i - 1, w - weight[i], memo);
java.explanation: Take branch recurses on i-1 with reduced capacity — encodes 'use each item once'.
Store the resolved best before returning so this state is never recomputed.

python.explanation: Caches solve by its (i, w) arguments automatically — the cleanest top-down memo in Python.
Best of include vs exclude. Note: deep recursion can hit Python's ~1000 default limit — prefer tabulation for large n.

edgeCases.behavior: Every take branch is blocked; memo[i][0] = 0 for all i — returns 0.
solve(0, W) can't take it, recurses to solve(-1, W) = 0 → answer 0.

pitfalls: Using 0 as the 'uncomputed' sentinel — collides with the valid answer 0; use -1.
Sizing the memo as W instead of W+1 — capacity 0..W is W+1 distinct columns.
In Python, deep top-down recursion can exceed the ~1000 recursion limit on large n — tabulation avoids the stack entirely.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up Table + 1-D Space Optimization (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Build the 2-D table, then collapse to 1-D and stress that the weight loop must run DESCENDING.
hints: Instead of recursing, fill a grid dp[i][w] = best value using the first i items within capacity w. dp[0][*] = 0.
For each item i and each capacity w: dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w] if it doesn't fit, else max(dp[i-1][w], value[i-1] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i-1]]).

Each row only reads the row above, so you can keep a single dp[w]. To still read the 'previous item' values, iterate w from W DOWN to weight[i] — descending order keeps dp[w - weight] referring to the old (item not yet taken) value.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The 2-D table has n × (W+1) cells, each filled in O(1) → O(nW) time. Because every row depends only on the one above it, a single rolling array of size W+1 suffices → O(W) space, no recursion stack.
approaches.explanation:
Build the answers from the ground up in a grid where `dp[i][w]` is the best value obtainable from the first `i` items within capacity `w`. Row 0 (no items) is all zeros. For each later item, every cell asks the same take-or-skip question as the recursion, but now both subproblems are already sitting in the row directly above.

**The 2-D recurrence, in table terms.** For item `i` (1-indexed into the table) with weight `wt` and value `val`: if `wt > w` the item can't fit, so `dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]` (inherit the skip value). Otherwise `dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], val + dp[i-1][w - wt])` — the best of skipping versus taking. The answer is `dp[n][W]`.

**Collapsing to one row.** Notice `dp[i][*]` only ever reads `dp[i-1][*]`. That means we don't need the whole grid — a single array `dp[w]` that we overwrite per item is enough, *if* we're careful about order.

**Why the 1-D loop must go DESCENDING — the crux of the whole problem.** When we process item `i` over a single array, `dp[w - wt]` must still hold the value from *before* this item was considered (the `dp[i-1]` row). If we iterate `w` ascending, we'd update `dp[w - wt]` first and then read it at `dp[w]` — meaning item `i` could be counted a second time, which is the *unbounded* knapsack answer. Iterating `w` from `W` down to `wt` guarantees `dp[w - wt]` is still the old value when we read it, so each item is used at most once. This single loop direction is the entire difference between 0/1 and unbounded knapsack.

**Why dp[0] stays 0.** With no items chosen, every capacity yields value 0; that bottom row anchors all the maxima above it, just as `dp[0]=0` anchors Coin Change.
approaches.insight: 0/1 Knapsack is the root of a whole family — Subset Sum, Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum, Last Stone Weight II are all this exact grid with the objective swapped (feasibility, equality, count). And the descending 1-D sweep is the portable trick: ascending = reuse allowed (unbounded), descending = once each (0/1). Memorize that one sentence and you can re-derive half the DP catalogue.

Default to the skip value carried from the previous item's row.
Take branch reads row i-1 (item not yet used), so it's counted at most once.

java.explanation: DESCENDING is the crux: dp[w - weight] still holds the pre-item value, enforcing 0/1. Ascending would allow reuse (unbounded).

Best of skip vs take, take reading strictly from the previous row.
Reverse range = descending sweep. This single direction is what keeps each item single-use.

edgeCases.behavior: Inner loop never runs (W < weight[i]); dp stays all zeros → answer 0.
No w satisfies w >= weight[i], dp untouched → 0.
dp[W] = max(0, value) = value — the item exactly fills the bag.

pitfalls: Iterating weight ASCENDING in the 1-D version — silently computes the unbounded answer by reusing items.
Reading dp[i][w - wt] (current row) instead of dp[i-1][w - wt] in the 2-D version — also reuses the item.
Off-by-one on the table size — use (n+1) × (W+1) and map item i to weight[i-1].
Looping w only down to 0 in the 1-D version — fine, but stopping at weight[i] is cleaner and avoids a negative index check.

commonMistakes: Iterating capacity ascending in the 1-D optimization, which reuses items and yields the unbounded-knapsack value.
Using the current item's row instead of the previous row in the take branch.
Treating 0 as 'uncomputed' in the memo when 0 is a valid maximum value.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ascending weight loop in the 1-D version
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Iterating w from low to high updates dp[w - weight] before you read it, so the same item is folded in twice — that's unbounded knapsack, not 0/1. Descending order preserves the previous-item values.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reading the current row in the 2-D take branch
commonMistakesDetailed.why: dp[i][w - wt] is being computed in this same pass, so it may already include item i — reusing it. The take branch must read dp[i-1], the previous item's row.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sentinel collides with a valid 0
commonMistakesDetailed.why: An empty or all-too-heavy knapsack scores 0, so 0 cannot also mean 'this memo cell is unfilled'. Use -1 (or a separate boolean grid).
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int[][] memo = new int[n][W + 1]; // defaults to 0
if (memo[i][w] != 0) return memo[i][w];

followupVariations.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
followupVariations.hint: 0/1 knapsack on feasibility: can a subset hit exactly total/2? Boolean dp[w], iterate descending.

followupVariations.title: Target Sum
followupVariations.hint: Assign + or − to each number — reduces to counting subsets with a fixed sum, a 0/1 knapsack count DP.

followupVariations.title: Last Stone Weight II
followupVariations.hint: Split stones into two groups with minimal difference — a 0/1 knapsack maximizing weight up to total/2.

followupVariations.title: Unbounded Knapsack
followupVariations.hint: Same value-maximizing setup but items are reusable — flip the 1-D weight loop to ascending.

patternNote: Canonical 0/1 knapsack — the root of the take-or-skip DP family. Recognize it whenever you choose a subset to optimize value under one capacity constraint with each item usable once. Same grid powers Subset Sum, Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum, and Last Stone Weight II; the descending 1-D sweep is what makes it '0/1' rather than unbounded.
